session.title: The States Enter the Assembly — Volume III Opens

primarySource.publisher: Parliament Digital Library, Lok Sabha Secretariat

transcriptReference.publisher: Constitution of India / Centre for Law and Policy Research
transcriptReference.note: Used for paragraph-level navigation and speaker segmentation; Parliament Digital Library remains canonical.

speakers.name: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
speakers.positionSummary: Welcomes representatives of Indian States, notes the British transfer-of-power deadline and outlines an accelerated committee-to-drafting timetable while warning that the political settlement may still require a constitution for only part of India.

speakers.name: B. L. Mitter
speakers.positionSummary: Presents the States as integral to India, supports a strong Centre and argues that constitutional design must accommodate the States' institutional variety without treating them as isolated sovereignties.

speakers.name: K. M. Panikkar
speakers.positionSummary: Treats the arrival of States representatives as a historic symbol of all-India constitution-making and rejects claims that their participation resulted from coercion.

speakers.name: P. Govinda Menon
speakers.stance: People of States belong in India
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that the people of the States always saw themselves as Indians and highlights Cochin's elected representation and explicit refusal to pursue separate independence.

speakers.name: T. Vijayaraghavachariar
speakers.positionSummary: Urges members from Provinces and States to work as representatives of India as a whole rather than as delegates of narrow territorial interests.

speakers.name: Jai Narain Vyas
speakers.positionSummary: Welcomes the collapse of institutional barriers between British India and the States and commits States representatives to constitution-making for India as a whole.

speakers.name: Raja Lal Shiva Bahadur Singh
speakers.positionSummary: Credits Rewa with enabling Central Indian representation and urges neighbouring States to join the Assembly quickly.

speakers.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
speakers.stance: Negotiated entry under a Union framework
speakers.positionSummary: Reports the negotiations with the Chamber of Princes, defends the agreed procedure for representation and stresses that State participation is voluntary but carries the responsibilities and benefits of joining the Union-making process.

speakers.name: Somnath Lahiri
speakers.positionSummary: Asks how many attending States representatives were elected rather than nominated and later objects that late notice prevented amendments to the States Committee resolution.

speakers.name: Kailas Nath Katju
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that rulers and States will be safest by joining an Indian Union and grounding their legitimacy in the trust of their own people.

speakers.name: G. Durgabai
speakers.positionSummary: Moves the election of two additional Steering Committee members from among representatives of Indian States rather than waiting for all reserved State seats to be filled.

speakers.name: H. V. Kamath
speakers.positionSummary: Initially proposes filling only one State-reserved Steering Committee seat because most States representatives are still absent, then withdraws after Nehru's assurance that further representation can be added later.

speakers.name: N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar
speakers.positionSummary: Presents the Union-subject report but asks the House not to debate it yet because League participation, States representation and impending political decisions may force a fresh examination of federal powers.

speakers.name: R. K. Sidhwa
speakers.positionSummary: Seeks assurance that the Union-subject report will still be open to discussion when the revised or subsequent report comes before the Assembly.

speakers.name: Several Members
speakers.positionSummary: Collective responses recorded when resolutions are adopted or procedural permissions are granted.

interventions.summary: The President opens the third session by recording the deaths of three members, including K. L. Mazumdar of Baroda, who died while travelling to attend the Assembly.
Rajendra Prasad formally welcomes representatives of Indian States and frames their participation as necessary to the Assembly's national constitutional task.

The President says Britain's intention to transfer power by June 1948 adds urgency. He sketches a compressed sequence: principle-setting committees, Assembly approval, drafting, and an effort to finalise the Constitution within 1947.
interventions.excerpt: we must proceed in a business-like way

interventions.summary: He warns that the Assembly may ultimately have to frame a constitution for only part of India and that territorial division cannot be ruled out as political negotiations continue.
B. L. Mitter thanks the House, describes the States as integral to India and argues for a strong Union that can accommodate the States' very different political and administrative conditions.
K. M. Panikkar calls the presence of States representatives historically symbolic, thanks the Negotiating Committee and rejects suggestions that the States were coerced into joining.

P. Govinda Menon argues that the people of the States never considered themselves separate from India. He presents Cochin's elected route into the Assembly and its ruler's commitment to remain part of India.
T. Vijayaraghavachariar asks members from States and Provinces to see themselves as members for all India and to frame a constitution capable of standing the test of time.
Jai Narain Vyas says States subjects had long been structurally excluded and celebrates their entry into the Assembly as artificial walls between the two Indias begin to fall.
Raja Lal Shiva Bahadur Singh says Rewa's participation prevented Central India from going unrepresented and urges other States to join soon.
The President reads a formal message from the Coorg Legislative Council wishing the Assembly success in completing an agreed Constitution.

Nehru moves that the States Committee report be recorded and explains the limited negotiating mandate: distribution of up to 93 States seats and the method of returning their representatives, while clarifying the Union framework and the Assembly's non-interference in internal State monarchy questions.

He describes the rapid agreement on seat distribution, acknowledges grouping difficulties and explains the compromise that at least half of States representatives should be elected through representative institutions or another electoral method.
Nehru urges the House not to let immediate political passions distort long-term constitutional design and argues that practical constitutional work should continue despite disruptive forces.
Somnath Lahiri asks how many States representatives attending the sitting were elected and how many were nominated.
Kailas Nath Katju says the variety of princely States should not obscure the historical pull toward an Indian Union and argues that rulers' security ultimately depends on the trust of their people.

The President notes Lahiri's complaint about late notice, puts the States Committee resolution to the House, records its adoption and answers that eleven of the sixteen attending States representatives were elected and five nominated.
G. Durgabai moves to elect two additional Steering Committee members from among States representatives, using Rule 40's reserved-State mechanism while leaving two further reserved places for later.

Kamath proposes filling only one seat because most States representatives are still absent. Nehru argues the Steering Committee needs working members now; Kamath withdraws after being assured that later additions remain possible.
The President sets the deadline for nominations and, if needed, the time and place for election of the additional Steering Committee members.

N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar presents the Committee on Union Subjects report but explicitly postpones substantive debate. He says League participation, fuller States representation and impending political decisions may require the Centre's subjects, concurrent field and Union-unit relations to be re-examined.
interventions.excerpt: not be taken as the final Report

interventions.summary: Ayyangar says the Union-subject committee will likely need to work with proposed Union-Constitution and Provincial-Constitution committees, especially if political decisions force departure from the Cabinet Mission framework.
The House unanimously condones the committee's two-day reporting delay and permits a further report if later political and constitutional developments require one.
R. K. Sidhwa asks whether the present Union-subject report will still be open to discussion later. The President confirms that members will have the opportunity when the matter returns.
The President fixes an early start for 29 April and tells members to submit amendments to the Fundamental Rights Committee report before the evening deadline.
